item.title: From off-target to on-demand: Precision engineering and translational evaluation of next-generation base editors.
item.abstract: Due to the increasing demand for clinical gene therapy and the limitations of current treatment methods, there is an urgent need to develop gene-editing tools that are safer, more precise, and more clinically implementable. Deaminase-based base editors have emerged as gene-editing platforms with significant therapeutic potential because they can achieve precise single-base substitutions without inducing DNA double-strand breaks. However, the challenges of applying base editing in clinical practice extend beyond whether the intended edit can be achieved. The critical question is whether the editing system can reliably provide predictable, controllable, and verifiable outcomes across complex sequence contexts, diverse cell environments, and actual delivery conditions. This review focuses on the engineering optimization and clinical translation of base editors. We first systematically analyze the major factors affecting the clinical translation of base editors across four dimensions: editing efficiency, editing precision, safety, and delivery, together with the corresponding optimization strategies. We then summarize the applications of artificial intelligence and computational approaches in base editor design, screening, and risk assessment. We further discuss the ex vivo and in vivo pathways for clinical translation, including their respective requirements for product quality and safety evaluation. Finally, based on representative clinical programs, we discuss how editing performance, safety, and delivery factors influence development decisions for candidate base-editing systems across different therapeutic contexts, and propose minimum reporting recommendations to improve the consistency of key data and cross-study comparability.

item.title: Shared α-helix chimeraffibodies enable linker-free bispecific protein design.
item.abstract: Small protein scaffolds enable precise targeting but often rely on flexible linkers that increase conformational heterogeneity and immunogenic liabilities. Here we develop Chimeraffibodies (CABs), a linker-free bispecific scaffold class that encodes interdomain geometry through seamless α-helix sharing. CABs are designed by AlphaSync, a structure-design framework that defines domain orientation through closed-form exhaustive local rigid-body superposition and ProteinMPNN-based sequence refinement. Using HER2-binding affibody and an albumin-binding domain, we generated 861CM, which preserved parental paratopes while enforcing a defined shared-helix architecture. Structural, biophysical and cellular analyses demonstrated stable assembly, cooperative target recruitment and retained affinity, with HSA binding of ∼14.3 pM and HER2 binding of 610 pM in the albumin-bound state. In vivo imaging revealed sustained tumor localization, reduced hepatic and renal background and improved organ-to-tumor contrast. CABs establish helix sharing as a geometry-encoded strategy for generating compact, homogeneous, and pharmacokinetically optimized bispecific proteins.

item.title: Engineering of the High-Precision Cas12m Dual Base Editor-Loaded Virus-like Particles for A-to-G and C-to-T Conversions.
item.abstract: Background/Objectives: CRISPR/Cas-dependent base editing enables the precise correction of genomic sequences by direct modification of DNA bases without creating potentially mutagenic DNA double-strand breaks. Base editing is considered a therapeutic approach for rare monogenic disorders or viral infections. However, many variants of base editors suffer from limited specificity because they induce bystander edits within a broad editing window. However, nucleotide substitution is sufficient to correct a mutation or to achieve a therapeutic effect. Methods: PCR, cloning by restriction digest, and ligation were used to create genetic constructs. The editing efficiency was evaluated using NGS. Virus-like particles were produced in HEK293T cells using transient expression. VLPs were visualized by electron microscopy. Results: Using dual base editors that induce C-to-T and A-to-G substitutions, we show that high editing precision can be achieved by engineering the linker between the MmCas12m domain and the deaminase domain of the editor. By testing different linker sequences, we have created high-precision dual base editors with narrowed editing windows that can edit a single nucleotide at a target position with high accuracy. Conclusions: We found that shortening the linker to an acceptable length provides a single-nucleotide substitution in vitro with minimal bystander activity (less than 0.8%), while the high-precision MmCas12m dual base editor retains up to 90% of the editing efficiency of the original base editor. These high-precision base editors will be useful in cases where high precision is required, and editing of adjacent nucleotides is undesirable.

item.title: JustEvo: A Prior-Guided Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Multifunctional Protein Directed Evolution.
item.abstract: Machine-learning-guided directed evolution can reduce the experimental burden of protein engineering by prioritizing variants before they are tested. In practice, however, many campaigns begin with few or no target-specific measurements, face choices about how to use heterogeneous protein-model priors, and require functional improvement to be balanced with developability properties such as expression and stability. Here, we present JustEvo, a closed-loop framework for low-data and multifunctional protein evolution. Before experimental measurement data are available, JustEvo nominates an informative first experimental batch using a mutation-prior model or a property-specific predictor. After measurements are obtained, it trains surrogate experts on multiple protein representations and adaptively combines their predictions according to their agreement with the current experimental fitness ranking. We evaluated these components using an EVOLVEpro-derived MoE validation data set and a ProteinGym-derived DMS collection split into a cold-start validation data set and a reserved benchmark data set. On the 81-landscape benchmark data set, JustEvo achieved higher final-round top 5 average fitness than EVOLVEpro and RelaVDEP under the same finite-budget acquisition protocol, with normalized scores of 0.862 for JustEvo, 0.849 for EVOLVEpro, and 0.818 for RelaVDEP. We further adapted JustEvo for fluorescent-protein optimization as a multiobjective design task. In this setting, objective-specific surrogate models were used to rank candidates by their predicted joint performance across coupled properties. We tested this extension on four in silico GFP landscapes and an experimental EYFP closed-loop campaign, where JustEvo expanded the fluorescence-stability Pareto front and increased Pareto hypervolume by 872.1%. These results show that coordinating prior-guided initialization, adaptive mixture-of-experts integration and objective-aware candidate ranking can improve protein variant selection under limited assay budgets.

item.title: CRISPR-based functional screening of noncoding regulatory elements.
item.abstract: The vast majority of trait-associated genetic variants reside in noncoding cis-regulatory elements (CREs), yet most regulatory sequences remain functionally uncharacterized. CRISPR-based screens enable direct perturbation of CREs in their native genomic context and have expanded into a diverse toolkit, including CRISPRi/CRISPRa, nuclease-mediated editing, base editing, prime editing, and continuous mutagenesis. Moreover, these approaches can be paired with phenotypic, transcriptomic, or chromatin readouts at single-cell resolution. However, a limitation of conventional pooled CRISPR screens is that cells are assigned by sgRNA identity rather than by the genotype installed. New genotype-resolved approaches address this gap by directly reading the edited endogenous sequence. Because sequence variants in CREs are associated with human disease, continued development of CRISPR-based technologies may help advance new therapies. In this review, we discuss diverse CRISPR-based modalities and their limitations, emerging genotype-resolved techniques, their applications in gene therapy, and computational approaches for predicting the function of regulatory sequences.

item.title: High-Throughput FRET Affinity Screening Technique (HTFAST) for Cell-Free Expressed Binding Protein Characterization.
item.abstract: The rapid engineering of binding proteins is increasingly driven by cell-free, machine-learning-guided optimization. However, high-throughput, quantitative characterization of binding affinity remains a major bottleneck, particularly for proteins expressed in cell-free systems without purification. Here, we present High-Throughput FRET Affinity Screening Technique (HTFAST) for rapid affinity characterization of binders expressed directly in crude E. coli cell-free protein expression reactions. HTFAST leverages Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) between cell-free expressed fluorescent-protein-fused binders and dye-labeled antigens to enable real-time, quantitative measurement of equilibrium dissociation constants. We systematically optimized fluorophore pairs and labeling parameters using the SpyTag003-SpyCatcher003 model system. HTFAST reliably quantified nanomolar binding affinities in crude lysates for the SpyTag003-SpyCatcher003 model system. It also resolved affinities spanning low-nanomolar to hundreds-of-nanomolar for nanobodies against multiple antigens, including CD4, HER2, and HSA. We further benchmarked HTFAST against a panel of five SARS-CoV-2 RBD nanobodies, demonstrating HTFAST's ability to rank binders targeting the same antigen with affinities correlating strongly with reported BLI/SPR measurements. Finally, we demonstrate that both binding partners can be expressed directly in CFE, further streamlining screening workflows. Overall, HTFAST provides a scalable, quantitative, and cell-free-compatible approach for high-throughput affinity screening, well-suited for DBTL protein engineering campaigns.

item.title: Structure-Function Relationships of Cid1 Poly(U) Polymerase: Catalysis, Substrate Recognition, Engineering, and Applications.
item.abstract: RNA 3'-end modification is an important regulatory mechanism that influences RNA processing, stability, localization, function, and degradation. Beyond its biological roles, RNA 3'-end modification has become a valuable tool in biotechnology, enabling applications in RNA labelling, sequencing, engineering and oligonucleotide synthesis. Terminal nucleotidyltransferases are key enzymes responsible for template-independent nucleotide addition to RNA molecules. Among these enzymes, Schizosaccharomyces pombe Cid1, a poly(U) polymerase, has emerged as an important model for understanding RNA-specific terminal nucleotidyltransferase activity. Structural and biochemical studies have revealed how nucleotide recognition, metal-ion-dependent catalysis, RNA positioning, and conformational dynamics regulate Cid1-mediated uridylation. Recent advances in protein engineering, molecular simulation, machine learning, and generative protein design have further expanded Cid1 functionality, generating variants with improved activity, altered substrate specificity, and potential applications in enzymatic RNA synthesis. This review summarizes the biological functions, structural characteristics, catalytic mechanisms, protein engineering strategies, and emerging biotechnological applications of Cid1, as well as the remaining challenges, highlighting its potential as a programmable platform for RNA 3'-end functionalization and enzymatic RNA oligonucleotide synthesis.

item.title: From Mechanistic Models to AI Synergy: A Roadmap for Predictive and Personalized Biology.
item.abstract: Two paradigms now drive the life sciences. One is the explanatory depth of mathematical modeling, the other the predictive power of artificial intelligence. For decades, mechanistic models have offered a rigorous, hypothesis-driven framework for dissecting biological processes, while AI has proven itself at finding patterns in the large, high-dimensional datasets of modern biology. Each has delivered major advances on its own. Together they promise a synthesis that could redefine the boundaries of biological inquiry. In this review we propose a three-part taxonomy of integration strategies, namely AI-accelerated mechanistic modeling, mechanism-informed AI, and hybrid models spanning one-directional sequential coupling and bidirectional iterative systems, and we survey their applications in systems and synthetic biology, pharmacology and drug discovery, epidemiology, and neuroscience. We then examine seven challenges that stand in the way: interpretability, data sparsity, causality, identifiability, computational scale, multimodal integration, and validation and generalization, and we close with a view of biological digital twins, causal discovery engines, and automated science. Our argument is that combining these approaches is the principal task for a new generation of interdisciplinary scientists who aim to build a predictive and mechanistic science of life.

item.title: ΔNAzyme: A Foundational QM/MM Δ-Machine Learning Potential for Nucleic Acid Enzyme Catalysis.
item.abstract: Nucleic acid enzymes (NAzymes), including ribozymes, DNAzymes, and XNAzymes, are programmable biocatalysts that catalyze diverse chemical reactions and provide unique platforms for investigating catalysis and engineering molecular function. Their central roles in biology and evolution, together with emerging applications in biotechnology, synthetic biology, and medicine, have created an urgent need for predictive computational design frameworks. Although multiscale computational enzymology integrating ab initio quantum mechanics can, in principle, provide predictive insight into these systems, current approaches remain computationally prohibitive for large, complex NAzymes and high-throughput design workflows. Machine learning potentials have the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of multiscale modeling approaches, but QM/MM contexts in which the MM environment is highly polarizing remain challenging. Nucleic acid enzymes present a particularly demanding case: experimentally relevant predictions require an accuracy that semiempirical QM/MM methods alone cannot reliably deliver in their often large, highly charged, metal-dependent active sites. Building on the range-corrected QM/MM Δ-machine learning potential (ΔMLP) framework, we develop ΔNAzyme, a foundational ΔMLP for nucleic acid enzyme reactions. We generate a training set of QM/MM simulations spanning diverse nucleic acid enzyme classes, with energies and forces computed at both the reference (DFTB3) and target (PBE0/6-31G*) levels of theory, yielding a correction on top of DFTB3 that recovers PBE0 quality results. We train models using both the Deep Potential and MACE architectures. The MACE model exhibits enhanced transferability, which we attribute to the equivariant, many-body message-passing framework. Free energy profiles from case-study reactions validate ΔNAzyme against target-level results and show that the model supports efficient fine-tuning to new nucleic acid enzyme systems with minimal additional data.

item.title: Protein Self-Assembly as a Design Principle for Enzyme Immobilisation in Biocatalysis.
item.abstract: Enzyme immobilisation is essential for translating biocatalytic processes from the laboratory to industrial applications by improving enzyme stability, recovery, and reuse. It underpins sustainable processes in pharmaceuticals, biofuels, and food production, but conventional immobilisation strategies involve inherent trade-offs. Covalent attachment prevents enzyme leaching but may distort the active site, whereas physical adsorption better preserves enzyme conformation but allows enzyme leaching. Furthermore, carrier-based methods frequently encounter mass-transfer limitations and may require external cross-linkers, hindering broader industrial application. Recent advances in synthetic biology and materials science have accelerated the development of protein-based materials for biocatalysis. This review examines protein self-assembly as a unifying design principle for enzyme immobilisation, enabling programmable assembly under relatively mild conditions to overcome key limitations of conventional strategies. We discuss naturally derived structures such as bacterial microcompartments and engineered systems including virus-like particles, elastin-like polypeptides, and SpyTag/SpyCatcher, which support programmable enzyme organisation and enable compartmentalised multi-enzyme cascade reactions. Building on this, a major focus is placed on catalytically active inclusion bodies (CatIBs). As robust, intrinsically self-immobilised protein aggregates, CatIBs represent a simplified, carrier-free platform offering potential process and cost advantages for industrial biocatalysis.

item.title: Small genomes, big lessons: What viruses teach us about structure-based riboregulation.
item.abstract: RNA viruses encode multiple layers of information within a single molecule, which functions simultaneously as a template for protein synthesis and as a structured regulatory RNA. These structures control key aspects of viral gene expression, govern host interactions, and mediate immune evasion. Although the prevalence of RNA structure in viral genomes is now well established, only recently have functional and mechanistic studies begun to uncover how these elements act as regulatory modules that shape infection outcomes. With their compact genomes and experimentally tractable life cycles, RNA viruses represent powerful model systems for uncovering the fundamental building blocks of riboregulation and illuminating principles of gene control conserved across eukaryotes. Here, we review current mechanistic understanding of RNA structure-based regulation across diverse viral families and draw parallels to structure-mediated gene control in eukaryotic transcriptomes, highlighting RNA structure as a central regulatory layer in gene expression with broad therapeutic and synthetic biology potential.

item.title: AI-Facilitated Discovery of Microbiome-Originated Antimicrobial Peptides: A Perspective on Combating Antibiotic Resistance Within Public Health and Food Safety Frameworks.
item.abstract: The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) demands innovative therapeutic strategies beyond conventional antibiotics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly those originating from the human, animal, and environmental microbiome, represent a promising frontier within public health microbiology and microbial food safety. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have revolutionized the discovery pipeline, enabling high-throughput mining of metagenomic data and de novo generation of novel peptide sequences. This perspective review synthesizes recent breakthroughs in AI-driven discovery of microbiome-originated AMPs, examines their preclinical efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens under One Health and climate-sensitive frameworks and application in infectious disease treatment and discusses translational challenges including pharmacokinetics, toxicity, manufacturing scalability, and applications in food preservation and water safety. We argue that the convergence of microbiome science, deep learning, and synthetic biology positions AI-discovered AMPs as viable next-generation interventions against antibiotic resistance across human, animal, and environmental domains.

item.title: Molecular Biology and Synthetic Biology-Guided Development of Recognition and Reporting Elements of Biosensor.
item.abstract: Microbial cell biosensors are capable of detecting fluctuations in the concentrations of substances both inside and outside the cell, as well as changes in the external environment, and can generate measurable signal outputs. Microbial cell biosensors are characterized by low cost, simple operation, and high specificity. The rapid advancement of synthetic biology has significantly propelled the development and practical application of microbial cell biosensors. In this chapter, we provide a comprehensive summary of the composition and working principles of microbial cell biosensors. Additionally, we introduce various strategies and the latest progress in modifying biorecognition element and reporting elements using molecular biology and synthetic biology techniques in recent years. This book chapter offers new insights and valuable references for the research and development of microbial cell biosensors.

item.title: SynBioFooDB: a comprehensive resource for synthetic biology-driven food biomanufacturing.
item.abstract: Enabled by synthetic biology and metabolic engineering, microbial biomanufacturing is reshaping the production of food-related compounds by offering sustainable alternatives to resource-intensive extraction and conventional chemical synthesis. However, information linking food-related compounds to biosynthetic pathways and microbial biomanufacturing evidence remains fragmented across the literature and poorly represented in existing food-oriented resources, hindering cross-study comparison, evidence synthesis, and rational design of microbial production systems. Here, we present SynBioFooDB (https://synbiofoodb.biodesign.ac.cn/), a knowledgebase dedicated to synthetic biology-driven food biomanufacturing. SynBioFooDB integrates 74 237 food-related compounds with standardized chemical identities and annotations covering food occurrence, bioactivity, toxicity, and regulatory information. It further provides expert-curated biomanufacturing evidence for 1054 compounds from 5592 publications, linking microbial hosts, substrates, genetic modifications, and quantitative production metrics through structured and traceable records. The database also contains 2002 literature-reported biosynthetic pathways for 971 compounds, enabling comparison of alternative precursors, enzyme combinations, and pathway architectures. For compounds without literature-reported pathways, SynBioFooDB provides computationally predicted candidate pathways to facilitate pathway prioritization and experimental evaluation. By integrating compound-level context, biomanufacturing evidence, and biosynthetic pathway information, SynBioFooDB supports systematic exploration, comparison, and rational design of microbial production strategies for food-related compounds.
